blocks.content: The Strategy Design Pattern is a behavioral pattern that lets you swap out how something gets done without changing the code that asks for it to be done.
Think of it as a plug-in system. The context does not care which algorithm runs it just hands the work off to whatever strategy is currently plugged in.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245787652-dbcc956e.png

["The same task can be done in multiple ways and the choice needs to change on the fly","You are tired of if-else chains that keep growing every time a new approach is added","You want each algorithm neatly boxed in its own class, not tangled up with everything else"]

blocks.content: Let's build a simple example and see how Strategy cleans things up.
1. The Problem: Sorting a List of Students
blocks.text: 1. The Problem: Sorting a List of Students

blocks.content: Imagine you are building a student management system. One feature you need is sorting students but the sorting criteria keeps changing depending on what the user wants:
["Sort by Name","Sort by Grade","Sort by Age","Sort by Roll Number"]
Your first attempt might look like this:
Client Code
This works for now. But watch what happens as requirements grow.
Where This Falls Apart
1. Violates Open/Closed Principle Every new sorting option means cracking open StudentSorterNaive and adding another branch. A class that should be stable keeps getting modified.
2. Bloated Conditional Logic The if-else chain grows with every new sort type. The method becomes long, hard to read, and easy to break.

3. Hard to Test Every sorting algorithm is buried inside one giant method. To test grade sorting you have to wire up the entire sorter and pass the right string. There is no way to test each algorithm on its own.
4. Risk of Duplication If another screen in the app needs student sorting, you copy this logic across. Now you have two places to update every time something changes.
5. Too Much Responsibility StudentSorterNaive knows every single sorting algorithm in detail. It should only be responsible for triggering the sort not owning every version of it.
What We Actually Need
A better design should:

["Give each sorting algorithm its own dedicated class","Let new sort options be added without touching any existing code","Allow the sorter to work without knowing which algorithm is running","Make every algorithm independently testable in isolation","Support swapping sort strategies at runtime based on user choice"]
items: Give each sorting algorithm its own dedicated class
Let new sort options be added without touching any existing code
Allow the sorter to work without knowing which algorithm is running
Make every algorithm independently testable in isolation
Support swapping sort strategies at runtime based on user choice

blocks.content: This is exactly what the Strategy Pattern delivers.
2. Understanding the Strategy Pattern
The Strategy Pattern defines a family of algorithms, boxes each one up in its own class, and lets you swap them in and out freely. The algorithm changes the code that uses it does not.
Two core ideas define it:
1. Encapsulated Algorithms Every algorithm lives in its own class behind a shared interface. The logic is self-contained and completely isolated from everything around it.
2. Runtime Swapping The context holds a reference to the interface, not any specific class. You can plug in a different strategy at any point without touching the context at all.

Real-World Analogy

 Think about how you might sort a pile of exam papers. You have several options:

  • Sort by name alphabetically for the attendance sheet
  • Sort by grade for the results board
  • Sort by age for a demographic report
  • Sort by roll number for the register

Each of these is a sorting strategy. You are the context you decide which approach fits the situation. The task of "sorting papers" never changes. Only the method you pick does.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245787736-e701fd5d.png
The Three Participants
1. Strategy Interface SortStrategy The shared contract every algorithm must fulfill. It declares one method sort() and that is all the context ever needs to know about it.
2. Concrete Strategies SortByName, SortByGrade, SortByAge Each class owns exactly one sorting algorithm and nothing else. They are fully interchangeable because they all speak the same interface.

3. Context StudentSorter The class that actually gets called by the rest of the app. It holds a reference to a SortStrategyand delegates the sorting work entirely to it. It does not know or care which strategy is plugged in it just calls sort() and lets the strategy handle the rest.
3. How It Works
The Strategy workflow is simple. The context does not change only the strategy plugged into it does.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245787860-0936fbb2.png
Step 1:The client creates a concrete strategy for exampleSortByName.
Step 2:The client passes it toStudentSorterthrough the constructor or a setter.
Step 3:The context stores it as aSortStrategyreference it never sees the concrete class.
Step 4:When sorting is needed, the context callssort()on the strategy and lets it do the work.
Step 5:To change behavior, the client swaps in a new strategy. The context code does not change at all.
4. Implementing the Strategy Pattern
Let's refactor the student sorter using the Strategy Pattern. One class per algorithm, zero if-else chains.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245787968-d3a43195.png
Step 1: Define the Strategy Interface
Step 2: Implement Concrete Strategies
SortByName
SortByAge
SortByRoll
Each class owns exactly one algorithm and nothing else.SortByGradeknows about grades.SortByAgeknows about ages. Neither knows the other exists.
Step 3: Create the Context Class
The context is deliberately simple. It stores a strategy, lets you swap it, and delegates the sort. That is all it does.
Step 4: Client Code
No conditional logic inside StudentSorter. Adding a new sort like SortByAttendance means writing one new class that implements SortStrategy. Nothing else changes.
What We Gained

["Open/Closed Principle Add new sort types by writing new classes, never by modifying existing ones","Single Responsibility Each strategy class does one thing only","Testability Every algorithm can be tested on its own with zero setup overhead","Runtime flexibility Swap the sort strategy at any point during execution","No string dispatch Type-safe strategy objects replace fragile string comparisons","Composition over inheritance Sorter and strategies are fully independent of each other"]
items: Open/Closed Principle Add new sort types by writing new classes, never by modifying existing ones
Single Responsibility Each strategy class does one thing only
Testability Every algorithm can be tested on its own with zero setup overhead
Runtime flexibility Swap the sort strategy at any point during execution
No string dispatch Type-safe strategy objects replace fragile string comparisons
Composition over inheritance Sorter and strategies are fully independent of each other
